public_rationale: IIHS research released July 23, 2026 found lower crash involvement rates for the Waymo driverless operations studied during 2021–2024 [e1]. Waymo-authored research published May 2, 2025 reported lower injury-related crash rates over 56.7 million rider-only miles through January 2025 [e2]. These findings do not separately establish fewer fatalities attributable to deployment [e1, e2]. AFB's June 2026 report, with fieldwork ending October 15, 2025, recorded accessibility barriers and reported that only 36% of surveyed AV riders could afford rides whenever needed or wanted [e3]. It does not establish substantial, sustained independence gains for many blind, older and disabled people [e3]. The evidence therefore leaves the combined forecast unresolved: it establishes neither both promised benefits nor their long-run impossibility [e1, e2, e3].
limitations: The safety findings apply to the studied Waymo operations and do not separately establish a fatality reduction [e1, e2].
The AFB findings report rider experiences and affordability, without establishing sustained independence gains at meaningful scale across the named populations [e3].
Present access barriers do not establish that long-run benefits cannot occur [e3].

public_payload.normalized_proposition: In the long run, driverless cars will save lives and give the blind, elderly, and disabled far more autonomy.

statement.excerpt: Does that mean that society should give up on building driverless cars? Absolutely not. In the long run, they will save lives, and also give many people, such the blind, elderly, and disabled, have far more autonomy over their own lives.
statement.document_title: Will Tesla ever “Solve” Full Self Driving?

from_speaker: far more autonomy over their own lives
our_interpretation: In the long run supplies no calendar deadline.
Driverless cars includes services that transport passengers without a human driver; this benefits claim does not explicitly require Level 5.
Save lives means fewer deaths than would otherwise occur for comparable travel, including effects on other road users.
Far more autonomy means substantial, sustained gains in independent travel and access to activities for many people in the named groups.
Both the safety and independence components must be established to support the combined forecast.
criteria.support_condition: Credible real-world evidence establishes reduced fatalities attributable to driverless deployment and substantial, sustained independent-mobility gains for many blind, older, and disabled people.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Decisive evidence establishes that the promised long-run benefits cannot occur. Present shortcomings or a limited deployment's failure do not alone contradict an undated forecast.

evidence.excerpt: The results provide further evidence that Waymo’s current L4 vehicles have lower crash involvement rates than human drivers.
evidence.explanation: The study of 2021–2024 records supports a safety benefit for Waymo's studied operations; the event date marks the final study year. Crash reductions do not independently establish the forecast's fatality and mobility components.

evidence.excerpt: Cyclist, Motorcycle, Pedestrian, Secondary Crash, and Single Vehicle crashes were also statistically reduced for the Any-Injury-Reported outcome.
evidence.explanation: This Waymo-authored study examines 56.7 million rider-only miles through January 2025 and reports favorable injury outcomes. It strengthens the safety case but does not separately establish reduced deaths or broad independence gains.

evidence.excerpt: Regardless of disability status, only 36% of AV riders said they could afford to pay for an AV whenever they wanted or needed one.
evidence.explanation: The survey records enthusiasm alongside affordability and accessibility barriers. Fieldwork ended October 15, 2025; the report specifies June 2026 publication, so June 30 is a conservative availability bound rather than an asserted publication day.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: Credible exposure-adjusted evidence of reduced fatalities attributable to driverless deployment, including effects on other road users, plus substantial, sustained independence gains at meaningful scale among blind, older and disabled people. Mobility studies should measure independent travel, access, affordability and usability. Decisive evidence that the promised long-run benefits cannot occur would instead contradict the forecast.
